items.stem: What colour is thymolphthalein in an alkaline solution?
items.answer: blue
items.markingKey: Thymolphthalein: colourless in acid, blue in alkali.

items.stem: Explain why universal indicator is more useful than litmus for comparing two acids.
items.answer: Universal indicator shows a range of colours corresponding to pH values, so it shows how acidic each solution is; litmus only shows acid or alkali.

items.stem: Explain why a pH meter can give more precise results than universal indicator paper.
items.answer: It gives a numerical reading (often to 0.01) rather than relying on judging a colour against a chart.

items.stem: Universal indicator is added to 3 solutions. A: rain water turns universal indicator yellow; B: toothpaste turns universal indicator blue; C: sodium hydrogencarbonate solution turns universal indicator blue. Suggest a pH for each and classify each as strongly acidic, weakly acidic, neutral, weakly alkaline or strongly alkaline. State which solution would turn thymolphthalein blue.
items.answer: A: pH ≈ 6, weakly acidic; B: pH ≈ 9, weakly alkaline; C: pH ≈ 8, weakly alkaline. Thymolphthalein blue: none (no strongly alkaline solution)
items.markingKey: A: pH ≈ 6, weakly acidic; B: pH ≈ 9, weakly alkaline; C: pH ≈ 8, weakly alkaline. Thymolphthalein blue: none (no strongly alkaline solution). 1 mark per solution [3]; thymolphthalein [1]

items.stem: Universal indicator is added to 4 solutions. A: oven cleaner turns universal indicator purple (violet); B: stomach acid turns universal indicator red; C: vinegar turns universal indicator red; D: sodium chloride solution turns universal indicator green. Suggest a pH for each and classify each as strongly acidic, weakly acidic, neutral, weakly alkaline or strongly alkaline. State which solution would turn thymolphthalein blue.
items.answer: A: pH ≈ 13, strongly alkaline; B: pH ≈ 2, strongly acidic; C: pH ≈ 3, strongly acidic; D: pH ≈ 7, neutral. Thymolphthalein blue: A
items.markingKey: A: pH ≈ 13, strongly alkaline; B: pH ≈ 2, strongly acidic; C: pH ≈ 3, strongly acidic; D: pH ≈ 7, neutral. Thymolphthalein blue: A. 1 mark per solution [4]; thymolphthalein [1]

items.stem: Diego tests four household and laboratory solutions from a kitchen in Jakarta: dilute hydrochloric acid, soap solution, orange juice, bleach. (a) State the colour of methyl orange in the most acidic solution. (b) Explain the difference between an alkali and a base. (c) Suggest which solution could be used to treat a bee sting (acidic) and why.
items.answer: (a) red (b) alkali is a soluble base (c) soap solution: a weak alkali neutralises the acid without damaging skin

items.stem: What colour is methyl orange in an acidic solution?
items.answer: red
items.markingKey: Methyl orange: red in acid, yellow in alkali.

items.stem: Describe how to measure the pH of a solution using universal indicator paper.
items.answer: Use a clean glass rod to put a drop of the solution on the paper; compare the colour with the pH colour chart.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a base and an alkali.
items.answer: A base is any substance that neutralises an acid (e.g. a metal oxide or hydroxide); an alkali is a base that dissolves in water.

items.stem: Universal indicator is added to 3 solutions. A: pure water turns universal indicator green; B: oven cleaner turns universal indicator purple (violet); C: cola drink turns universal indicator red. Suggest a pH for each and classify each as strongly acidic, weakly acidic, neutral, weakly alkaline or strongly alkaline. State which solution would turn thymolphthalein blue.
items.answer: A: pH ≈ 7, neutral; B: pH ≈ 13, strongly alkaline; C: pH ≈ 3, strongly acidic. Thymolphthalein blue: B
items.markingKey: A: pH ≈ 7, neutral; B: pH ≈ 13, strongly alkaline; C: pH ≈ 3, strongly acidic. Thymolphthalein blue: B. 1 mark per solution [3]; thymolphthalein [1]

items.stem: Universal indicator is added to 4 solutions. A: oven cleaner turns universal indicator purple (violet); B: aqueous ammonia turns universal indicator purple (violet); C: vinegar turns universal indicator red; D: bleach turns universal indicator purple (violet). Suggest a pH for each and classify each as strongly acidic, weakly acidic, neutral, weakly alkaline or strongly alkaline. State which solution would turn thymolphthalein blue.
items.answer: A: pH ≈ 13, strongly alkaline; B: pH ≈ 11, strongly alkaline; C: pH ≈ 3, strongly acidic; D: pH ≈ 12, strongly alkaline. Thymolphthalein blue: A, B, D
items.markingKey: A: pH ≈ 13, strongly alkaline; B: pH ≈ 11, strongly alkaline; C: pH ≈ 3, strongly acidic; D: pH ≈ 12, strongly alkaline. Thymolphthalein blue: A, B, D. 1 mark per solution [4]; thymolphthalein [1]

items.stem: Omar tests four household and laboratory solutions from a kitchen in Toronto: lemon juice, dilute hydrochloric acid, orange juice, cola drink. (a) Predict the colour of universal indicator in each solution. (b) Suggest which solution could be used to treat a bee sting (acidic) and why.
items.answer: (a) lemon juice: red; dilute hydrochloric acid: red; orange juice: orange; cola drink: red (b) a weak alkali such as baking soda: a weak alkali neutralises the acid without damaging skin
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per two correct [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: Mateo tests four household and laboratory solutions from a kitchen in Singapore: tomato juice, pure water, toothpaste, vinegar. (a) State the colour of methyl orange in the most acidic solution. (b) Describe how a more precise pH value could be obtained. (c) Explain the difference between an alkali and a base. (d) Suggest which solution could be used to treat a bee sting (acidic) and why.
items.answer: (a) red (b) use a calibrated pH meter / probe (c) alkali is a soluble base (d) toothpaste: a weak alkali neutralises the acid without damaging skin

items.stem: What is an acid, according to the proton definition?
items.answer: a proton (H⁺) donor
items.markingKey: Acids donate H⁺ ions.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a strong acid and a concentrated acid.
items.answer: Strength refers to the degree of dissociation (strong = fully ionised); concentration refers to how much acid is dissolved per dm³. A weak acid can be concentrated.

items.stem: Explain why 0.1 mol/dm³ ethanoic acid has a higher pH than 0.1 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid.
items.answer: Ethanoic acid is weak and only partially dissociates, so the concentration of H⁺ ions is lower, giving a higher pH.

items.stem: Freya compares 0.500 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid with 0.500 mol/dm³ ethanoic acid. Results: pH – hydrochloric acid 0.3, ethanoic acid 2.5; time for a 2 cm piece of magnesium ribbon to react – hydrochloric acid 25 s, ethanoic acid 150 s; electrical conductivity – hydrochloric acid high, ethanoic acid low. Explain why magnesium reacts faster with the strong acid.
items.answer: higher concentration of H⁺ ions, so more frequent collisions

items.stem: Chloe compares 1.00 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid with 1.00 mol/dm³ ethanoic acid. Results: pH – hydrochloric acid 0.0, ethanoic acid 2.4; time for a 2 cm piece of magnesium ribbon to react – hydrochloric acid 25 s, ethanoic acid 200 s; electrical conductivity – hydrochloric acid high, ethanoic acid low. (a) Explain the difference in conductivity. (b) Calculate how many times greater the H⁺ concentration is in the hydrochloric acid, using the pH values.
items.answer: (a) more ions in the strong acid solution to carry charge (b) about 250 times
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) pH difference 2.4; each unit = factor 10 → 10^2.4 ≈ 250 [2]

items.stem: Elena compares 0.100 mol/dm³ nitric acid with 0.100 mol/dm³ ethanoic acid. Results: pH – nitric acid 1.0, ethanoic acid 2.9; time for a 2 cm piece of magnesium ribbon to react – nitric acid 20 s, ethanoic acid 160 s; electrical conductivity – nitric acid high, ethanoic acid low. (a) Explain the difference in pH. (b) Calculate how many times greater the H⁺ concentration is in the nitric acid, using the pH values.
items.answer: (a) nitric acid is a strong acid, fully dissociated; ethanoic acid is weak, partially dissociated, so lower [H⁺] (b) about 79 times
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: strong fully dissociated; 1 mark: weak partially so lower [H⁺] [2] (b) pH difference 1.9; each unit = factor 10 → 10^1.9 ≈ 79 [2]

items.stem: Ethan investigates the differences between nitric acid and ethanoic acid of the same concentration. (a) Define a strong acid and a weak acid. (b) Write the ionic equation for the reaction of an acid with calcium carbonate.
items.answer: (a) strong: completely dissociated in water; weak: partially dissociated (b) CaCO₃(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Ca²⁺(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)

items.stem: Omar investigates the differences between nitric acid and ethanoic acid of the same concentration. (a) Write equations to show the dissociation of nitric acid and of ethanoic acid. (b) Evaluate which acid is better for the cleaning company.
items.answer: (a) HNO₃ → H⁺ + NO₃⁻ (complete); CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ (partial) (b) strong acid works faster but is more corrosive/hazardous; ethanoic acid is safer for surfaces and users but slower – justified choice
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark each side; 1 mark conclusion [3]

items.stem: What is a base, according to the proton definition?
items.answer: a proton (H⁺) acceptor
items.markingKey: Bases accept H⁺ ions.

items.stem: Which acid is a weak acid?
items.answer: ethanoic acid
items.markingKey: Ethanoic acid only partially dissociates.

items.stem: Explain why magnesium reacts more slowly with ethanoic acid than with hydrochloric acid of the same concentration.
items.answer: Ethanoic acid is only partially ionised, so the concentration of H⁺ ions is lower and collisions between H⁺ and Mg are less frequent.

items.stem: Explain why ammonia is described as a base when it reacts with hydrogen chloride.
items.answer: Ammonia accepts a proton (H⁺) from HCl to form the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺.

items.stem: The pH of an acid solution increases from 5 to 7 when it is diluted. Describe how the hydrogen ion concentration changes, giving the factor.
items.answer: It decreases by a factor of 100 (10 for each pH unit).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: decreases; 1 mark: factor 10^2 = 100 [2]

items.stem: Priya compares 0.0100 mol/dm³ nitric acid with 0.0100 mol/dm³ ethanoic acid. Results: pH – nitric acid 2.0, ethanoic acid 3.4; time for a 2 cm piece of magnesium ribbon to react – nitric acid 25 s, ethanoic acid 200 s; electrical conductivity – nitric acid high, ethanoic acid low. Predict whether the same total volume of hydrogen would be produced if excess magnesium were used with equal volumes of each acid. Explain.
items.answer: yes: same number of moles of acid; the weak acid continues to dissociate as H⁺ is used up

items.stem: Tomás compares 0.100 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid with 0.100 mol/dm³ ethanoic acid. Results: pH – hydrochloric acid 1.0, ethanoic acid 2.9; time for a 2 cm piece of magnesium ribbon to react – hydrochloric acid 30 s, ethanoic acid 120 s; electrical conductivity – hydrochloric acid high, ethanoic acid low. (a) Explain why magnesium reacts faster with the strong acid. (b) Explain the difference in conductivity. (c) Calculate how many times greater the H⁺ concentration is in the hydrochloric acid, using the pH values.
items.answer: (a) higher concentration of H⁺ ions, so more frequent collisions (b) more ions in the strong acid solution to carry charge (c) about 79 times
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) [1] (c) pH difference 1.9; each unit = factor 10 → 10^1.9 ≈ 79 [2]

items.stem: Mei investigates the differences between hydrochloric acid and ethanoic acid of the same concentration. (a) Write equations to show the dissociation of hydrochloric acid and of ethanoic acid. (b) Identify the proton donor and the proton acceptor in that reaction.
items.answer: (a) HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻ (complete); CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ (partial) (b) H⁺ (from the acid) donor; carbonate ion acceptor
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) [1]

items.stem: A cleaning company in Singapore must choose between hydrochloric acid and ethanoic acid (vinegar) for removing limescale (calcium carbonate). (a) Define a strong acid and a weak acid. (b) Write equations to show the dissociation of hydrochloric acid and of ethanoic acid. (c) Identify the proton donor and the proton acceptor in that reaction.
items.answer: (a) strong: completely dissociated in water; weak: partially dissociated (b) HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻ (complete); CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ (partial) (c) H⁺ (from the acid) donor; carbonate ion acceptor
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) 1 mark each [2] (c) [1]

items.stem: What are the products when a metal reacts with a dilute acid?
options: a salt, water and carbon dioxide
items.answer: a salt and hydrogen
items.markingKey: Metal + acid → salt + hydrogen.

items.stem: Explain how the name of the salt formed in an acid reaction depends on the acid used.
items.answer: The acid provides the anion: hydrochloric acid → chlorides, sulfuric acid → sulfates, nitric acid → nitrates; the metal or base provides the cation.

items.stem: Explain why copper does not react with dilute hydrochloric acid but magnesium does.
items.answer: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it cannot displace hydrogen from the acid; magnesium is above hydrogen.

items.stem: Name the products formed when magnesium reacts with nitric acid, and describe one observation.
items.answer: magnesium nitrate and hydrogen; fizzing as hydrogen is given off; the metal gets smaller
items.markingKey: products [1]; observation [1]

items.stem: Lucas adds copper(II) carbonate to hydrochloric acid. Describe what is observed, name the products and write the balanced symbol equation.
items.answer: Fizzing (effervescence) as carbon dioxide is given off; the solid dissolves. Products: copper(II) chloride and water and carbon dioxide. CuCO₃ + 2HCl → CuCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂
items.markingKey: observation [1]; products named [1]; CuCO₃ + 2HCl → CuCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂: formulae [1], balanced [1]

items.stem: Samuel adds an excess of magnesium oxide to warm nitric acid to make crystals of magnesium nitrate. (a) Write the balanced symbol equation, with state symbols. (b) Explain why an excess of the solid is used.
items.answer: (a) MgO + 2HNO₃ → Mg(NO₃)₂ + H₂O (b) to make sure all the acid reacts; excess removed by filtration
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark formulae; 1 mark balancing [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: Describe a test to show that a gas given off when an acid reacts with a solid is carbon dioxide.
items.answer: Bubble the gas through limewater; it turns milky (cloudy white).

items.stem: Explain why farmers add calcium hydroxide (slaked lime) to acidic soil.
items.answer: It is a base that neutralises the excess acid in the soil, raising the pH so crops grow better.

items.stem: Explain how you could tell, from observations alone, whether a white solid added to hydrochloric acid is a metal carbonate or a metal oxide.
items.answer: A carbonate fizzes (effervescence) because CO₂ is produced, which turns limewater milky; an oxide dissolves without fizzing (only salt + water).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: carbonate fizzes / CO₂; 1 mark: oxide no gas; 1 mark: limewater test [3]

items.stem: Name the products formed when magnesium oxide reacts with sulfuric acid, and describe one observation.
items.answer: magnesium sulfate and water; the solid dissolves, forming a solution (coloured if a copper/iron salt)
items.markingKey: products [1]; observation [1]

items.stem: Lina adds iron(II) carbonate to sulfuric acid. Describe what is observed, name the products and write the balanced symbol equation.
items.answer: Fizzing (effervescence) as carbon dioxide is given off; the solid dissolves. Products: iron(II) sulfate and water and carbon dioxide. FeCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → FeSO₄ + H₂O + CO₂
items.markingKey: observation [1]; products named [1]; FeCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → FeSO₄ + H₂O + CO₂: formulae [1], balanced [1]

items.stem: Amara adds an excess of magnesium hydroxide to warm sulfuric acid to make crystals of magnesium sulfate. (a) Describe what is observed during the reaction. (b) Explain why an excess of the solid is used. (c) Identify the ion responsible for the acidic properties of the acid.
items.answer: (a) the solid dissolves (b) to make sure all the acid reacts; excess removed by filtration (c) H⁺(aq)

items.stem: In an IGCSE practical lesson, magnesium sulfate is made by reacting magnesium carbonate with sulfuric acid. (a) Describe what is observed during the reaction. (b) Explain why an excess of the solid is used. (c) Describe how pure, dry crystals are obtained.
items.answer: (a) fizzing (effervescence) as carbon dioxide is given off; the solid dissolves (b) to make sure all the acid reacts; excess removed by filtration (c) filter; heat filtrate to crystallisation point; cool; filter and dry crystals

items.stem: Which oxide is amphoteric?
items.answer: zinc oxide
items.markingKey: ZnO reacts with both acids and alkalis.

items.stem: Explain why sulfur dioxide is classified as an acidic oxide.
items.answer: It reacts with alkalis (e.g. sodium hydroxide) to form a salt and water, and dissolves in water to give an acidic solution.

items.stem: Describe how you could show that aluminium oxide is amphoteric.
items.answer: Add some to dilute hydrochloric acid and some to warm aqueous sodium hydroxide; it dissolves (reacts) in both.

items.stem: Write the balanced symbol equation, with state symbols, for the reaction of iron(III) oxide with hydrochloric acid, and state what this reaction shows about the type of oxide.
items.answer: Fe₂O₃(s) + 6HCl(aq) → 2FeCl₃(aq) + 3H₂O(l); iron(III) oxide is basic (it reacts with an acid)
items.markingKey: Fe₂O₃(s) + 6HCl(aq) → 2FeCl₃(aq) + 3H₂O(l): formulae [1]; balanced [1]; states [1]; type of oxide [1]

items.stem: Four oxides are tested with acid and alkali. oxide P: with dilute HCl – no reaction, with aqueous NaOH – no reaction; oxide Q: with dilute HCl – reacts, with aqueous NaOH – no reaction; oxide R: with dilute HCl – no reaction, with aqueous NaOH – reacts; oxide S: with dilute HCl – reacts, with aqueous NaOH – reacts. Classify each oxide as acidic, basic, amphoteric or neutral.
items.answer: P: neutral; Q: basic; R: acidic; S: amphoteric
items.markingKey: P: neutral; Q: basic; R: acidic; S: amphoteric. 1 mark each [4]

items.stem: Ines investigates the oxides magnesium oxide (MgO), iron(III) oxide (Fe₂O₃), nitrogen dioxide (NO₂). (a) Explain how the type of oxide is linked to the position of the element in the Periodic Table. (b) Describe an experiment to show that an oxide is amphoteric.
items.answer: (a) metals on left → basic; non-metals on right → acidic; some (Al, Zn) amphoteric (b) add to dilute acid and to aqueous NaOH separately; it reacts/dissolves in both

items.stem: Which type of oxide is formed by most non-metals?
items.answer: acidic
items.markingKey: Non-metal oxides react with alkalis.

items.stem: Explain why oxides of elements on the left of the Periodic Table are basic while those on the right are acidic.
items.answer: Metals (on the left) form basic oxides; non-metals (on the right) form acidic oxides; metallic character decreases across a period.

items.stem: Explain why calcium oxide is used to remove sulfur dioxide from power-station waste gases.
items.answer: Calcium oxide is basic and neutralises the acidic sulfur dioxide, forming calcium sulfite (and so reducing acid rain).

items.stem: Write the balanced symbol equation, with state symbols, for the reaction of zinc oxide with hydrochloric acid, and state what this reaction shows about the type of oxide.
items.answer: ZnO(s) + 2HCl(aq) → ZnCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l); zinc oxide is amphoteric (it reacts with an acid)
items.markingKey: ZnO(s) + 2HCl(aq) → ZnCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l): formulae [1]; balanced [1]; states [1]; type of oxide [1]

items.stem: Three oxides are tested with acid and alkali. oxide P: with dilute HCl – reacts, with aqueous NaOH – no reaction; oxide Q: with dilute HCl – no reaction, with aqueous NaOH – reacts; oxide R: with dilute HCl – no reaction, with aqueous NaOH – no reaction. Classify each oxide as acidic, basic, amphoteric or neutral.
items.answer: P: basic; Q: acidic; R: neutral
items.markingKey: P: basic; Q: acidic; R: neutral. 1 mark each [3]

items.stem: Write the balanced symbol equation, with state symbols, for the reaction of sodium oxide with hydrochloric acid, and state what this reaction shows about the type of oxide.
items.answer: Na₂O(s) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l); sodium oxide is basic (it reacts with an acid)
items.markingKey: Na₂O(s) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l): formulae [1]; balanced [1]; states [1]; type of oxide [1]

items.stem: Which pH value is neutral?
items.markingKey: pH 7 is neutral at 25 °C.

items.stem: Elena tests dilute hydrochloric acid and sodium hydrogencarbonate solution with universal indicator: they turn red and blue respectively. Suggest the pH of each and explain what the colours show about the solutions.
items.answer: dilute hydrochloric acid: pH ≈ 1 (strongly acidic); sodium hydrogencarbonate solution: pH ≈ 8 (weakly alkaline). The lower pH solution has a higher concentration of H⁺ ions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: both pH values; 1 mark: classification; total [2]

items.stem: Universal indicator is added to 3 solutions. A: milk turns universal indicator yellow; B: stomach acid turns universal indicator red; C: milk of magnesia turns universal indicator blue. Suggest a pH for each and classify each as strongly acidic, weakly acidic, neutral, weakly alkaline or strongly alkaline. State which solution would turn thymolphthalein blue.
items.answer: A: pH ≈ 6, weakly acidic; B: pH ≈ 2, strongly acidic; C: pH ≈ 10, weakly alkaline. Thymolphthalein blue: C
items.markingKey: A: pH ≈ 6, weakly acidic; B: pH ≈ 2, strongly acidic; C: pH ≈ 10, weakly alkaline. Thymolphthalein blue: C. 1 mark per solution [3]; thymolphthalein [1]

items.answer: A: pH ≈ 8, weakly alkaline; B: pH ≈ 6, weakly acidic; C: pH ≈ 12, strongly alkaline; D: pH ≈ 2, strongly acidic. Thymolphthalein blue: C
items.markingKey: A: pH ≈ 8, weakly alkaline; B: pH ≈ 6, weakly acidic; C: pH ≈ 12, strongly alkaline; D: pH ≈ 2, strongly acidic. Thymolphthalein blue: C. 1 mark per solution [4]; thymolphthalein [1]

items.stem: What is meant by a strong acid?
options: an acid that does not ionise
an acid with a pH of 7
an acid that is completely dissociated into ions in aqueous solution
items.answer: an acid that is completely dissociated into ions in aqueous solution
items.markingKey: Strong = fully ionised.

items.stem: Write equations to show the difference in dissociation of hydrochloric acid and ethanoic acid.
items.answer: HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻ (complete); CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ (partial, reversible).

items.stem: Explain, in terms of proton transfer, which species is the acid and which is the base in the reaction H₂SO₄(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → SO₄²⁻(aq) + 2H₂O(l).
items.answer: H₂SO₄ is the acid because it donates a proton (H⁺); OH⁻ is the base because it accepts the proton.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: acid identified as proton donor; 1 mark: base identified as proton acceptor [2]

items.stem: The pH of an acid solution increases from 3 to 5 when it is diluted. Describe how the hydrogen ion concentration changes, giving the factor.
items.answer: It decreases by a factor of 100 (10 for each pH unit).

items.answer: yes: same number of moles of acid; the weak acid continues to dissociate as H⁺ is used up

items.answer: (a) strong: completely dissociated in water; weak: partially dissociated (b) HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻ (complete); CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ (partial)
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Copper(II) carbonate reacts with nitric acid. What are the products?
items.answer: copper(II) nitrate + water + carbon dioxide
items.markingKey: salt + water + carbon dioxide: CuCO₃ + 2HNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + H₂O + CO₂.

items.stem: Explain how you could tell, from observations alone, whether a white solid added to sulfuric acid is a metal carbonate or a metal oxide.
items.answer: A carbonate fizzes (effervescence) because CO₂ is produced, which turns limewater milky; an oxide dissolves without fizzing (only salt + water).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: carbonate fizzes / CO₂; 1 mark: oxide no gas; 1 mark: limewater test [3]

items.answer: magnesium chloride and water; the solid dissolves
items.markingKey: products [1]; observation [1]

items.stem: 25.0 cm³ of 0.500 mol/dm³ potassium hydroxide is exactly neutralised by sulfuric acid of concentration 0.200 mol/dm³. 2KOH + H₂SO₄ → K₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Calculate the volume of acid needed and name the salt formed.
items.answer: 31.3 cm³; potassium sulfate
items.markingKey: n(alkali) = 0.0125 mol [1]; n(acid) = 0.00625 mol (ratio 2:1) [1]; V = 31.3 cm³ [1]; salt potassium sulfate [1]

items.stem: In a college laboratory, copper(II) chloride is made by reacting copper(II) carbonate with hydrochloric acid. (a) Write the balanced symbol equation, with state symbols. (b) Describe how pure, dry crystals are obtained. (c) Describe a test for the gas produced.
items.answer: (a) CuCO₃ + 2HCl → CuCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂ (b) filter; heat filtrate to crystallisation point; cool; filter and dry crystals (c) limewater turns milky (CO₂)
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark formulae; 1 mark balancing [2] (b) [3] (c) [1]

items.stem: Predict how silicon(IV) oxide, SiO₂, reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid and with aqueous sodium hydroxide, and explain your prediction.
items.answer: It is acidic: reacts with alkalis (but not acids) to form a salt and water; oxides of non-metals are usually acidic. Silicon is a non-metal, and non-metal oxides are usually acidic.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: classification; 1 mark: reactions with acid and alkali; total [2]

items.stem: Predict how sodium oxide, Na₂O, reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid and with aqueous sodium hydroxide, and explain your prediction.
items.answer: It is basic: reacts with acids (but not alkalis) to form a salt and water; oxides of metals are usually basic. Sodium is a metal, and metal oxides are basic or amphoteric.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: classification; 1 mark: reactions with acid and alkali; 1 mark: link to metal/non-metal [3]

items.stem: Write the balanced symbol equation, with state symbols, for the reaction of sulfur trioxide with sodium hydroxide solution, and state what this reaction shows about the type of oxide.
items.answer: SO₃(g) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na₂SO₄(aq) + H₂O(l); sulfur trioxide is acidic (it reacts with an alkali)
items.markingKey: SO₃(g) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na₂SO₄(aq) + H₂O(l): formulae [1]; balanced [1]; states [1]; type of oxide [1]

items.stem: Sipho investigates the oxides sulfur dioxide (SO₂), calcium oxide (CaO), iron(III) oxide (Fe₂O₃). (a) Classify each oxide as acidic, basic or amphoteric. (b) Name the products when a basic oxide reacts with an acid.
items.answer: (a) sulfur dioxide: acidic; calcium oxide: basic; iron(III) oxide: basic (b) a salt and water
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [3] (b) [1]

items.stem: What is an alkali?
options: a substance that produces H⁺ ions
items.answer: a soluble base
items.markingKey: Alkalis dissolve in water and produce OH⁻ ions.

items.stem: Sipho tests pure water and aqueous ammonia with universal indicator: they turn green and purple (violet) respectively. Suggest the pH of each and explain what the colours show about the solutions.
items.answer: pure water: pH ≈ 7 (neutral); aqueous ammonia: pH ≈ 11 (strongly alkaline). The higher pH solution has a higher concentration of OH⁻ ions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: both pH values; 1 mark: classification; total [2]

items.stem: Universal indicator is added to 3 solutions. A: sea water turns universal indicator blue; B: cola drink turns universal indicator red; C: sodium chloride solution turns universal indicator green. Suggest a pH for each and classify each as strongly acidic, weakly acidic, neutral, weakly alkaline or strongly alkaline. State which solution would turn thymolphthalein blue.
items.answer: A: pH ≈ 8, weakly alkaline; B: pH ≈ 3, strongly acidic; C: pH ≈ 7, neutral. Thymolphthalein blue: none (no strongly alkaline solution)
items.markingKey: A: pH ≈ 8, weakly alkaline; B: pH ≈ 3, strongly acidic; C: pH ≈ 7, neutral. Thymolphthalein blue: none (no strongly alkaline solution). 1 mark per solution [3]; thymolphthalein [1]

items.stem: Universal indicator is added to 4 solutions. A: stomach acid turns universal indicator red; B: oven cleaner turns universal indicator purple (violet); C: rain water turns universal indicator yellow; D: soap solution turns universal indicator blue. Suggest a pH for each and classify each as strongly acidic, weakly acidic, neutral, weakly alkaline or strongly alkaline. State which solution would turn thymolphthalein blue.
items.answer: A: pH ≈ 2, strongly acidic; B: pH ≈ 13, strongly alkaline; C: pH ≈ 6, weakly acidic; D: pH ≈ 10, weakly alkaline. Thymolphthalein blue: B, D
items.markingKey: A: pH ≈ 2, strongly acidic; B: pH ≈ 13, strongly alkaline; C: pH ≈ 6, weakly acidic; D: pH ≈ 10, weakly alkaline. Thymolphthalein blue: B, D. 1 mark per solution [4]; thymolphthalein [1]

items.stem: Ines tests four household and laboratory solutions from a kitchen in Accra: orange juice, pure water, oven cleaner, baking soda solution. (a) Predict the colour of universal indicator in each solution. (b) Identify any solutions that are alkaline and state the ion responsible. (c) Explain the difference between an alkali and a base.
items.answer: (a) orange juice: orange; pure water: green; oven cleaner: purple (violet); baking soda solution: blue (b) oven cleaner, baking soda solution – OH⁻ ions (c) alkali is a soluble base
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per two correct [2] (b) [2] (c) [1]

items.stem: Which ion is present in all aqueous solutions of acids?
items.answer: H⁺
items.markingKey: Acids produce H⁺(aq).

items.stem: Explain, in terms of proton transfer, which species is the acid and which is the base in the reaction HCl(g) + NH₃(g) → NH₄Cl(s).
items.answer: HCl is the acid because it donates a proton (H⁺); NH₃ is the base because it accepts the proton.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: acid identified as proton donor; 1 mark: base identified as proton acceptor [2]

items.stem: Explain, in terms of proton transfer, which species is the acid and which is the base in the reaction NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq).
items.answer: H₂O is the acid because it donates a proton (H⁺); NH₃ is the base because it accepts the proton.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: acid identified as proton donor; 1 mark: base identified as proton acceptor [2]

items.stem: Ines compares 0.0100 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid with 0.0100 mol/dm³ ethanoic acid. Results: pH – hydrochloric acid 2.0, ethanoic acid 3.4; time for a 2 cm piece of magnesium ribbon to react – hydrochloric acid 30 s, ethanoic acid 240 s; electrical conductivity – hydrochloric acid high, ethanoic acid low. Calculate how many times greater the H⁺ concentration is in the hydrochloric acid, using the pH values.
items.answer: about 25 times
items.markingKey: pH difference 1.4; each unit = factor 10 → 10^1.4 ≈ 25 [2]

items.stem: The pH of an acid solution increases from 2 to 4 when it is diluted. Describe how the hydrogen ion concentration changes, giving the factor.
items.answer: It decreases by a factor of 100 (10 for each pH unit).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: decreases; 1 mark: factor 10^2 = 100 [2]

items.stem: A cleaning company in Madrid must choose between sulfuric acid and ethanoic acid (vinegar) for removing limescale (calcium carbonate). (a) Predict which acid has the lower pH at the same concentration and explain why. (b) Write the ionic equation for the reaction of an acid with calcium carbonate.
items.answer: (a) sulfuric acid: higher [H⁺] because fully dissociated (b) CaCO₃(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Ca²⁺(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)

items.stem: Magnesium oxide reacts with sulfuric acid. What are the products?
items.answer: magnesium sulfate + water
items.markingKey: salt + water: MgO + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂O.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why farmers add calcium hydroxide (slaked lime) to acidic soil. (b) Explain how the name of the salt formed in an acid reaction depends on the acid used.
items.answer: (a) It is a base that neutralises the excess acid in the soil, raising the pH so crops grow better. (b) The acid provides the anion: hydrochloric acid → chlorides, sulfuric acid → sulfates, nitric acid → nitrates; the metal or base provides the cation.

items.stem: Name the products formed when copper(II) carbonate reacts with sulfuric acid, and describe one observation.
items.answer: copper(II) sulfate and water and carbon dioxide; fizzing (effervescence) as carbon dioxide is given off; the solid dissolves
items.markingKey: products [1]; observation [1]

items.stem: Zara adds magnesium to hydrochloric acid. Describe what is observed, name the products and write the balanced symbol equation.
items.answer: Fizzing as hydrogen is given off; the metal gets smaller. Products: magnesium chloride and hydrogen. Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂
items.markingKey: observation [1]; products named [1]; Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂: formulae [1], balanced [1]

items.stem: Amara adds an excess of magnesium hydroxide to warm sulfuric acid to make crystals of magnesium sulfate. (a) Write the balanced symbol equation, with state symbols. (b) Explain why an excess of the solid is used. (c) Explain why no gas is produced. (d) Identify the ion responsible for the acidic properties of the acid.
items.answer: (a) Mg(OH)₂ + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + 2H₂O (b) to make sure all the acid reacts; excess removed by filtration (c) a base reacts with acid to give only salt and water (d) H⁺(aq)
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark formulae; 1 mark balancing [2] (b) [2] (c) [1] (d) [1]

items.stem: Predict how sulfur dioxide, SO₂, reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid and with aqueous sodium hydroxide, and explain your prediction.
items.answer: It is acidic: reacts with alkalis (but not acids) to form a salt and water; oxides of non-metals are usually acidic. Sulfur is a non-metal, and non-metal oxides are usually acidic.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: classification; 1 mark: reactions with acid and alkali; total [2]

items.stem: Predict how nitrogen monoxide, NO, reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid and with aqueous sodium hydroxide, and explain your prediction.
items.answer: It is neutral: reacts with neither acids nor alkalis. Nitrogen is a non-metal, but a few non-metal oxides such as CO, NO and N₂O are neutral.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: classification; 1 mark: reactions with acid and alkali; 1 mark: link to metal/non-metal [3]

items.stem: Write the balanced symbol equation, with state symbols, for the reaction of copper(II) oxide with sulfuric acid, and state what this reaction shows about the type of oxide.
items.answer: CuO(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → CuSO₄(aq) + H₂O(l); copper(II) oxide is basic (it reacts with an acid)
items.markingKey: CuO(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → CuSO₄(aq) + H₂O(l): formulae [1]; balanced [1]; states [1]; type of oxide [1]

items.stem: Lucas investigates the oxides magnesium oxide (MgO), carbon dioxide (CO₂), iron(III) oxide (Fe₂O₃). (a) Classify each oxide as acidic, basic or amphoteric. (b) Predict the pH of a solution formed when an acidic oxide dissolves in water.
items.answer: (a) magnesium oxide: basic; carbon dioxide: acidic; iron(III) oxide: basic (b) below 7
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [3] (b) [1]
